title: How to Improve School Cultures, Part 4b: A Case Study in Earnest and Amicable Argument as PD cable-argument-as-pd/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Continuing his series on school culture, Stuart offers a concrete case of argument as professional development. Patty Sankey, a reading specialist in Wisconsin, adapted his 'pressing question of the month' idea so that her staff read articles around a single question tied to the school improvement plan, then argued at mixed-discipline tables about the most impactful strategies for closing achievement gaps. Stuart reads the design closely: a clear argumentative prompt, evidence from shared readings, a euphemistic label ('Academic Collaborative Conversations') to avoid baggage, and an individual application step at the end. Her report that staff became their own experts and were genuinely excited supports his claim that great school cultures are richly argumentative as well as safe.
points: A clear, argumentative prompt tied to the school improvement plan turns a lifeless planning document into something a staff is intellectually engaged by.
Reading shared articles for a month before the meeting grounds table arguments in evidence rather than opinion.
Calling the discussions 'Academic Collaborative Conversations' sidesteps the baggage of the word argument while keeping the substance of rational, evidence-based disagreement.
Ending with each teacher naming one change for one student moves PD from a big question to a manageable application, which busy teachers need for PD to create change.
The case suggests staffs can build their own expertise through reading and argument instead of paying outside experts.
quotes: So: arguments make for rich school cultures — not just arguments in our classrooms, but arguments in our meetings. But what does this actually look like? Thankfully, there's a school in Wisconsin that's laid out a pretty good example of this.

Now, notice: by asking for the most impactful strategies, Sankey set things up to get argumentative. (Good, clear prompts are critical in setting up good argumentative conversations.) It's also important to note that this question was directly linked with the school improvement plan at Patty's school. (Typically, SIPs can be lifeless, gargantuan things, so approaching them argumentatively is a smart move for getting a staff intellectually engaged.
(The articles help ensure that folks will make evidence-based arguments rather than relying on opinion.)

This is where the arguing happened. Even though Patty called these table conversations “Academic Collaborative Conversations” when she was leading the PD — and that was probably a smart move, as the word “argument” is so wrought with baggage that simply hearing it is bound to turn some PD participants off at first — make no mistake about it: these teachers were arguing. These conversations were rational, evidence-based, “let's get to the bottom of this” affairs — they were earnestly and amicably argumentative.

This final application piece is a smart way to move from the big, pressing question into a manageable, “can't miss” application. When teachers are as busy as we are, such applications are inseparable from PD that actually creates change.
There's no way around it: great school cultures aren't just safe — they're richly argumentative, too.
